newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's trade union fears new labour laws.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's trade union fears new labour laws.

text.p: The Alliance of Independent Trade Unions of Serbia said on Thursday that nearly 650,000 workers would be adversely affected by new labour laws, due to come into effect in 1997.

"Under the federal labour law, which abolishes paid compulsory leave, around 620,000-650,000 workers will remain completely unprotected," Slobodanka Brankovic, a member of the pro-government trade union's presidency, told Reuters.
She said the law made it easier to sack workers, as employees who lose their jobs will be entitled to up to five months pay instead of up to three years.
The breakup of the former Yugoslav federation in 1991 and nearly four years of sanctions against rump Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, crippled its once medium developed economy.
As industrial capacities became idle, hundreds of thousands of workers in large enterprises were sent on "compulsory leave", receiving some 60-70 percent of their salaries.
In September, official statistics registered the total number of employed in Yugoslavia at 2.06 million, of which 1.94 million were in Serbia. At the same time some 820,000 people were seeking work.
The data does not include the private sector.
Although sanctions were suspended in November 1995, economic recovery has been slow and industrial capacities are now running at around 40 percent of their pre-war level.
Managers of big state-controlled firms had been reluctant to lay off workers, fearing social unrest before the federal parliamentary elections held last Sunday.
But with the victory of the socialist-led leftist coalition, the coast is clear to implement long-promised market-oriented policies and abandon the protective function of large enterprises.
But Brankovic said the new labour laws would give too much powers to directors of large state-owned firms.
"The law is very restrictive towards workers. Too much power lies in the hands of directors," Brankovic said.

She conceded surplus labour was a problem, but said someone had to take over responsibility for these workers and the country needed to adopt a social programme urgently. -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 2224305
